title: Fish and Chips
subtitle: Beer-battered cod with twice-fried chips
excerpt: Thick white cod fillets in a crisp beer batter, served with thick-cut chips fried twice until golden and fluffy inside. The twice-fry is what makes pub-quality chips at home.
sourceNotes: Fish and chips became the dominant British takeaway dish in the second half of the nineteenth century, when mechanised fishing and railway distribution made fresh fish affordable throughout Britain. The beer batter is associated with northern England, while the south tended towards plain flour batter. The twice-fry chip method became standard in professional kitchens in the twentieth century and is now used in most good chip shops.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The first fry of the chips can be done up to two hours ahead. Keep them at room temperature. Finish the second fry just before serving.
recipe.temperatureNote: Deep-fry temperature controlled by thermometer, not oven

glossaryTerms.definition: A thin wet mixture of flour and liquid, used to coat food before frying. A beer batter for fish uses beer to introduce carbonation, which lightens the fried crust.

content.text: Fish and chips is thick white fish in a crisp

with twice-fried chips. The batter is made with beer, which carbonates lightly as it fries and gives it a delicate crunch rather than a solid casing. The chips are fried twice: first at a lower temperature to cook through, then at a higher temperature to crisp the outside. Cook the chips first, then the fish.
Use a large, deep saucepan and fill it no more than one-third deep with oil. This gives the oil room to bubble up when you lower the food in. Keep the lid of the pan close by.

items.prepNote: thick fillets, skin removed, about 180 g each

content.text: Cut the {{potato}} of potato into thick chips, about 1.5 cm by 1.5 cm. Rinse under cold water to remove surface starch, then pat dry.

Heat the oil in a large deep saucepan to 150°C. Lower the chips in batches using a slotted spoon. Fry for 5 to 6 minutes until cooked through but still pale. They should be soft when you press one. Drain on kitchen paper. This is the first fry.
Make the batter and coat the fish
Whisk {{plain-flour}} of flour with the salt in a large bowl. Pour in {{beer}} of cold beer gradually, whisking until smooth. The batter should be the consistency of double cream.
Pat the {{cod-fillet}} of cod fillets dry. Dust each fillet lightly with flour, then dip into the batter, letting the excess drip back.
Fry the fish and finish the chips

Raise the oil to 180°C. Lower the battered fish one at a time into the oil, holding it at the surface for a second before releasing so the batter sets and it does not stick to the bottom. Fry for 5 to 6 minutes until golden and crisp. Drain on kitchen paper.

Keep the oil at 180°C. Return the par-cooked chips to the oil in batches. Fry for 3 to 4 minutes until golden and crisp. This is the second fry. Drain on kitchen paper and season immediately with salt.

rows.symptom: Batter falls off the fish during frying
rows.cause: Fish not dried before battering, or oil not hot enough
rows.fix: Pat the fish completely dry before dusting with flour. The flour layer helps the batter stick. Check the oil is at 180°C before the fish goes in.

rows.symptom: Chips are soft rather than crisp after the second fry
rows.cause: Oil temperature dropped too much when the chips went in
rows.fix: Fry in smaller batches so the oil temperature recovers between additions. Let the oil come back to 180°C before the next batch.

rows.symptom: Batter is soggy rather than crisp
rows.cause: Beer was not cold, or batter made too far in advance
rows.fix: Use ice-cold beer. Make the batter just before using it; standing batter loses its lightness as the carbonation fades.

content.text: Fish and chips shops spread across industrial Britain in the second half of the nineteenth century as a cheap, fast meal for factory and mill workers. By the 1930s there were over 35,000 chip shops in Britain. The dish survived wartime rationing as one of the few items not controlled, which embedded it more deeply in British food culture than almost any other dish. Today the best chip shops in Britain still use beef dripping for the chips and fry them in a cast-iron range, but sunflower oil at home gives a clean, neutral result.
